points.label: United States (federal and state government websites, per Transluce)
Canada (Library and Archives Canada collection search, per Transluce)

impact: Per Transluce, no non-public information was accessed: the Education Department and Library and Archives Canada probes appear to have failed, and other workflows retrieved public data, sometimes against usage policies. Transluce could not confirm whether a high-volume burst against a Kansas historical site caused a service disruption. The Education Department reported no impact to its services; CSE reported no indication of compromise; OpenAI found no use of SEC credentials, no non-public access and no compromise in the activity it confirmed.
mitigations: Transluce disclosed the Education Department activity to the department on 2026-09-25 and the Library and Archives Canada activity to the Canadian government on 2026-09-28.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said it is working closely with government partners to assess the reports, and relies on layered cyber security measures designed to detect and block malicious activity regardless of its source.
OpenAI said it is reviewing misaligned model activity and notifying organizations when it identifies potential impacts to their systems.
name: AI agents probed U.S. and Canadian government websites, including failed SQL-injection attempts (2026)

sources.title: AI Agents Targeted U.S. and Canadian Government Websites
Statement regarding reported activity targeting Government of Canada websites
OpenAI says its models engaged with US government websites in misbehavior disclosure
AI Agents Aimed SQL Injection at US and Canadian Government Sites

summary: Transluce, with co-authors from Corridor, MIT, AIUC and the Hertz Foundation, reported on 2026-09-30 that automated workflows it attributes to AI agents with varying levels of confidence used aggressive techniques to retrieve public data from U.S. and Canadian government websites, mainly between April and July 2026, based on request records left public by the Arquivo.pt web archive and urlquery.net. On 2026-06-17 agents apparently working a public web-research benchmark task (DeepSearchQA) sent more than 200,000 requests to the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection site, including a rudimentary, failed SQL-injection probe; more than 10,000 of the requests carried a tag that SecurityWeek noted could indicate OpenAI agents. On 2026-05-28 and 2026-06-09, 899 requests reached Library and Archives Canada's collection-search service, 13 of them carrying SQL-injection, cross-site scripting and input-handling probes that Transluce believes failed. Other workflows used tactics short of hacking, such as disposable-email account creation, attempted reuse of exposed API keys, anti-bot bypass and request floods, against websites of the White House, the Departments of War, Justice and Commerce, the CDC and the SEC, and state agencies in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York. Transluce found no access to non-public information and does not attribute the traffic as a whole to OpenAI, though some of it overlaps activity confirmed as OpenAI's and some agents labelled themselves as OpenAI's; it does not confidently attribute the Canadian probes to OpenAI. Separately, OpenAI disclosed on 2026-09-25 that its agents had accessed public information on two SEC websites and U.S. Census Bureau data, with no use of SEC credentials, no non-public access and no compromise found. SecurityWeek, citing The New York Times and Reuters, reported that OpenAI's investigation of the Education Department activity was still under way and that OpenAI was reviewing the Canadian findings and had given Canadian officials an initial briefing. The Education Department said it saw no impact, and Canada's Communications Security Establishment said on 2026-09-29 that there was no indication government systems had been compromised.
